01.r: Points to the place the treasure is kept.

02.r: Gives the reason behind the two commands about treasure.

04.r: With 'your', marks the hearer's own treasure; English uses 'your' alone.

05.r: Whatever a person has laid up as his wealth.
05.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'a place of safe keeping'; by extension, what is kept there.

06.n: Singular in our Greek text, though the two verses before speak to 'you' in the plural; the saying turns to each listener. The Textus Receptus has the plural here, which the KJV's 'your' follows, against the ASV's singular 'thy'.

07.r: The same place as the treasure.

08.r: The heart is bound to follow the treasure.
08.n: A future tense, of what will certainly follow. The DRC's 'is' turns it into a present.

09.r: The heart joins the treasure in the same place.

10.r: With 'your', marks the hearer's own heart.

11.r: The centre of a person's desires and loyalties.
11.n: Abbott-Smith, after the bodily organ, gives the psychological sense: 'the seat of man's collective energies, the focus of personal life'. Here it is what a person cares for most.

12.r: The same single hearer as before.
12.n: Singular again; the Textus Receptus has the plural here too.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads ὑμῶν, 'your' (plural), in both places where our text has the singular σου. The KJV and Geneva follow it with 'your'; the DRC and ASV keep the singular with 'thy'.
